items.title: A small retriever
items.prose:
Build the retrieval half of a research assistant from nothing. Write `build_index(docs)` and `query(index, text, k)`.

- Words: lower-case runs of the letters a to z.
- Chunks: windows of 12 words starting every 8 words (overlap 4); stop once a window reaches the last word.
- Weights: drop the `STOP` words from each window, then TF-IDF over all windows (counts times $\ln\frac{1+n}{1+\text{df}} + 1$, $n$ windows), each window scaled to length 1.
- A query is weighted the same way with the windows' IDF. A document scores its best window's cosine.
items.question: Return the ids of at most $k$ documents with a score above 0, best first, ties to the lower id; no known word gives [].

tests.setup:
P = ['the board met in june and the auditors signed the accounts while the dividend held and the outlook stayed firm for the year though lenders flagged a covenant breach at corran', 'corran denies breach claim made today', 'a covenant was reset at dunmore']
IP = build_index(P)

import random
from llm_apps_ops_l1 import load_notes, make_reports, COMPANIES, TOPICS
NOTES = load_notes()['notes']
REPS = make_reports(NOTES)
DOCS = [r['text'] for r in REPS]
WHERE = {i: ri for ri, r in enumerate(REPS) for i in r['ids']}
_g = random.Random(99)
_c = [(c, t) for c in COMPANIES for t in TOPICS]
_g.shuffle(_c)
HQ = []
for c, t in _c[:24]:
    a, b = _g.sample(TOPICS[t], 2)
    HQ.append(('what about %s and %s or %s' % (c, a, b), sorted({WHERE[n['id']] for n in NOTES if n['company'] == c and n['topic'] == t})))
IX = build_index(DOCS)
def recall3():
    return sum(len(set(query(IX, q, 3)) & set(r)) / len(r) for q, r in HQ) / len(HQ)

widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Ten compare exact lists of document ids: five queries on a planted case of three documents, one of them all stop words, four questions on 30 long reports built from the 180-note file, and $k = 0$. The last needs mean recall at 3 of at least 0.5 over 24 hidden labelled questions on those reports.

mutants.symptom: Indexes each document whole, with no chunks.
Returns documents whose best score is 0.
Lists a document once for every matching window.
Steps windows by 12, so they do not overlap.

feedback.correct: Your retriever matches on every planted case and clears the recall bar on the hidden questions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: The planted breach sits in the last words of a long document: cut it into windows of 12 so the window holding the breach can win.
byKey.test-3: Return only documents with a score above 0: 'dunmore' is in one document only.
byKey.test-2: With STOP words left out, the short third document is the best match for 'covenant': drop STOP words from the windows and the query.
byKey.test-4: List each document once, scored by its best window.
byKey.test-6: Windows start every 8 words, so neighbours share 4: your second window starts at word 12.

explain.text: Chunking lets a passage, not its whole document, win; stop words and the per-document best score keep the list honest. The same steps sit under any retrieval-augmented tool.

Returns the standard deviation, not the standard error.

items.title: From question to passages
items.prose: A retrieval tool must be built once and then answer questions. Two of the steps below do not belong.
items.question: Put the steps in order and leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Cut each document into overlapping chunks
Fit the IDF on the chunks, with stop words left out
Store each chunk's TF-IDF vector, scaled to length 1
Turn the question into a vector with the stored IDF
Score every chunk by its cosine with the question
Return the top $k$ chunks' passages, best first
Fit a fresh IDF on the question's own words
lines.why: The question's own df is 1 for every word, which would weigh them all alike. The IDF comes from the chunks.

lines.text: Rank chunks by their raw dot product
lines.why: The raw dot product rewards long chunks; rank by cosine.

feedback.correct: Index first (chunks, IDF, vectors), then per question: vector, scores, top $k$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Build the index before any question arrives.

byKey.d1: The question's own words cannot give an IDF: every df is 1. Reuse the chunks' IDF.
byKey.d2: The dot product favours long chunks; use the cosine.

explain.text: The index is built once: chunk, fit IDF, store unit vectors. Each question then reuses that IDF, is scored by cosine and returns the top $k$.

items.title: A confident wrong answer
items.prompt: An analyst asks the desk's research assistant, a language model fed the top 3 passages from a TF-IDF search over 4,000 broker notes, whether a company's lenders have waived a covenant. It answers 'no' with confidence and cites two notes from last year; a waiver note from last month exists. Explain how much of the failure may be retrieval, how you would measure it, and what you would change.
items.model:
**Retrieval or reading.** The model can only use what it is handed. If the waiver note was not in the top 3, the failure is retrieval; if it was there and the model ignored it, the failure is reading. Check first: run the same query and see where the waiver note ranks.

**Likely retrieval causes.** The note may say 'lenders agreed to relax the leverage test' without the word 'waive', and word overlap misses synonyms. A long note indexed as one vector may bury the passage. Old notes that share more words can outrank a newer one.

**Measure.** Build labelled queries: 50 to 100 real questions with the passages that answer them, written by analysts and kept apart from any tuning. Report recall at 3 (the model reads 3) and MRR, with a standard error. Compare any change against the current search by per-query differences, not two headline numbers.

**Change.** Chunk notes into overlapping windows. Add an embedding search (LSA or a trained model) alongside TF-IDF so synonyms match. Add a date filter or recency boost when the question is about now, and return 'nothing found' when no score clears a floor. Re-measure on the held-out queries after each change.

rubric.text: Separates retrieval failure (the note not in the top 3) from reading failure (in the top 3 but ignored), and says how to tell which
Names at least two plausible retrieval causes, such as synonyms, a whole note as one vector, or recency
Proposes labelled queries kept apart from tuning, and recall at the number of passages read (3)
Compares changes by per-query differences with a standard error, not two headline numbers
Proposes concrete changes: chunking, an embedding search, a date filter or a 'nothing found' floor, each re-measured

items.title: Reading a search log
items.prose: A search tool's log covers 40 questions, one needed note each. The note was first at rank 1 for 18 questions, at rank 2 for 10 and at rank 3 for 4. For the other 8 it was outside the top 3 or never found.
items.question: What is recall at 3 over the 40 questions? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count questions whose note is in the top 3.

explain.text: $18 + 10 + 4 = 32$ of 40 questions have their note in the top 3, so recall at 3 is 0.80.

items.title: Choosing a chunk size
items.prose: A language model reads 4 chunks per question. Annual reports are 30,000 words; most answers sit in one paragraph of about 150 words. Labelled questions show recall at 4 of 0.81 with 300-word chunks and 0.62 with 3,000-word chunks.
items.question: Which choice is best supported?

options.text: 300-word chunks with some overlap, re-checked on held-out questions
3,000-word chunks, since the model then sees more text
options.why: Longer chunks dilute the paragraph's words, which is why recall fell to 0.62.

options.text: One vector per report, so nothing is cut
options.why: A paragraph in 30,000 words is a sliver of the vector; it would rarely rank.
Too short loses the context around an answer and cuts paragraphs apart; it needs measuring too.

feedback.correct: Chunks near the size of an answer score best, and the figure should hold on fresh questions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which size matched the answers, and which recall was higher?

explain.text: 300-word chunks sit near the 150-word answers and gave recall 0.81 against 0.62. Overlap protects answers on a boundary; held-out questions guard against having tuned the size to these ones.
